chunks: Al-Husayn ibn Muhammad, from Al-Sayyari, from Ahmad ibn Al-Fadl, from Yunus, from Al-Rida (peace be upon him) regarding
the dung-eating fish — he had asked him about it, so he said: 'It is to be kept for one day and one night'.
And Al-Sayyari said: 'This does not happen except at Basra'.

And he said regarding the chicken: 'It is to be confined for three days; and the duck for seven days; and the sheep for fourteen days; and the cow for thirty days; and the camel for forty days — then they are slaughtered'.

key_terms.البصرة: Basra — the city in Iraq, noted here as the location where dung-eating fish were particularly prevalent
key_terms.الجلال: Jalal — an animal that habitually eats human or animal waste/dung, rendering its meat ritually questionable until quarantined
key_terms.يُحبس: To be confined/detained — the animal must be kept away from impure food sources during the quarantine
key_terms.يُنتظر: To be kept/awaited — the jurisprudential term for the quarantine period (istibraa) required to purify a jalal animal

ai.seo_question: How long must dung-eating animals be quarantined before being slaughtered in Islamic law?
ai.summary: Imam al-Rida (AS) rules on the ritual purification period required for animals and fish that have been feeding on impure substances (jalal animals). The ruling establishes graded quarantine periods ranging from one day-and-night for fish, to forty days for camels, after which the animal may be lawfully slaughtered and consumed. Al-Sayyari adds a geographic note that the fish ruling specifically applies to Basra, where dung-eating fish were commonly found. This hadith reflects the Shia jurisprudential principle of tahara (ritual purity) as applied to food consumption.
